solution:
**(a) Work done by the gas.** For an isothermal expansion of \(n\) moles from volume \(V_1\) to \(V_2\),

\(W = nRT\ln\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = 2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)\)

Here \(n = 0.5\), \(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), \(T = 300\ \text{K}\), \(V_1 = 2\ \text{L}\) and \(V_2 = 6\ \text{L}\), so \(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 3\).

\(W = 2.303 \times 0.5 \times 8.31 \times 300 \times \log_{10}3\)

\(W = 2.303 \times 1246.5 \times 0.4771\)

\(W = 1370\ \text{J}\)

**(b) Heat supplied to the gas.** The process is isothermal, so the temperature and hence the internal energy of the ideal gas do not change:

\(\Delta U = 0\)

From the first law \(Q = \Delta U + W\),

\(\therefore Q = W = 1370\ \text{J}\)

All the heat supplied is used in doing external work.

(a) The work done in isothermal expansion is \(W = nRT \ln\left(\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\right)\)

Where \(n = 0.5\), \(V_{f} = 6\)L, \(V_{i} = 2\)L

\(W = 0.5\ \text{mol} \times \dfrac{8.319}{\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}} \times 300\,K \cdot \ln\left(\dfrac{6L}{2L}\right)\)

\(= 1.371\) kJ.

(b) From the first law of thermodynamics, the heat supplied in an isothermal process is spent to do work on a system. Therefore, \(Q = W = 1.371\) kJ.

Can you explain the significance of positive sign of the work done and the heat?
note: 0.5 x 8.319 x 300 x ln 3 = 1370.9 J with the stem's R = 8.319; 1.369 came from R = 8.31.

solution:
Work done in isobaric process given by \(W = P\Delta V = (V_{f} - V_{i})\).

\(V_{f} = 2V_{i}\) \(\therefore\) \(W = pV_{i}\).

\(V_{i}\) can be found by using the ideal gas equation for initial state.

\(P_{i} V_{i} = nRT_{i}\) for \(n = 1\) mol,

\(V_{i} = \dfrac{RT_{i}}{P_{i}} = 8.314 \times \dfrac{300}{1.01 \times 10^{6}} = 2.4695 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^{3}\)

\(\therefore W = 1.01 \times 10^{6} \times 2.4695 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(W = 2.494\) kJ
note: The stem's pressure is 1.01 MPa, not 1 MPa: V_i = 2.4695e-3 m^3; W = pV_i = 2494 J unchanged.

solution:
Given :
\( q_1 = -2\,\mu\text{C} = -2 \times 10^{-6} \) C, \( r_1 = 0.08 \) m
\( q_2 = +4\,\mu\text{C} = +4 \times 10^{-6} \) C, \( r_2 = 0.08 \) m
\( r = 16 \) cm \( = 0.16 \) m

a) Electrostatic potential energy of the system of two charges is

\( V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r} \)

\( = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (-2) \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{0.16} \)

\( = -0.45 \) J

b) In the electric field, total potential energy

\( (\text{PE}) = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} + q_1 V(\vec{r_1}) + q_2 V(\vec{r_2}) \)

\( E = \dfrac{-dV}{dr} \therefore V = \int -E\,dr = \int \dfrac{-A}{r^2}\,dr,\ V = \dfrac{A}{r} \)

\( \therefore \text{Total PE} = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} + \dfrac{A q_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{A q_2}{r_2} \)

\( = -0.45 + \dfrac{8 \times 10^{5} \times (-2 \times 10^{-6})}{0.08} + \dfrac{8 \times 10^{5} \times (4 \times 10^{-6})}{0.08} \)

\( = -0.45 - 20 + 40 \)

\( = 19.55 \) J
note: r1, r2 are 0.08 m (printed cm); U of the pair is -0.45 J (printed 0.45; the total 19.55 J already used -0.45).

solution:
Given :
\( C_1 = 8\,\mu\text{F} \), \( C_2 = 4\,\mu\text{F} \), \( C_3 = 1\,\mu\text{F} \), \( C_4 = 4\,\mu\text{F} \), \( C_5 = 4\,\mu\text{F} \)

The effective capacitance of \( C_4 \) and \( C_5 \) in parallel
\( = C_4 + C_5 = 4 + 4 = 8\,\mu\text{F} \)

The effective capacitance of \( C_3 \) and \( 8\,\mu\text{F} \) in series
\( = \dfrac{1 \times 8}{1 + 8} = \dfrac{8}{9}\,\mu\text{F} \)

The capacitance \( 8\,\mu\text{F} \) is in parallel with the series combination of \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \). Their effective combination is

\( \dfrac{C_1 C_2}{C_1 + C_2} + \dfrac{8}{9} \Rightarrow \dfrac{8 \times 4}{12} + \dfrac{8}{9} \Rightarrow \dfrac{32}{9}\,\mu\text{F} \)

This capacitance of \( \dfrac{32}{9}\,\mu\text{F} \) is in series with \( C \) and their effective capacitance is given to be \( 1\,\mu\text{F} \)

\( \dfrac{\dfrac{32}{9} \times C}{\dfrac{32}{9} + C} = 1 \)

\( \therefore \dfrac{32}{9} \times C = \dfrac{32}{9} + C \)

\( = \dfrac{32}{23} = 1.391\,\mu\text{F} \)

Energy stored in the capacitor with air

\( E_a = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 10^{-9} \times (400)^2 \)
\( = 24 \times 10^{-5} \) J

when the slab of dielectric constant 3 is introduced between the plates of the capacitor, the capacitance of the capacitor increases to
\( C' = kC \)
\( C' = 3 \times 3 \times 10^{-9} = 9 \times 10^{-9} \) F

Energy stored in the capacitor with the dielectric \( (E_d) \)

\( E_d = \dfrac{1}{2}C'V^2 \)

\( E_d = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times 10^{-9} \times (400)^2 \)
\( = 72 \times 10^{-5} \) J

On removing the slab, change in energy \( = E_a - E_d = (24 - 72) \times 10^{-5} \)
\( = -48 \times 10^{-5} \) J

There is, therefore, a decrease of \( 48 \times 10^{-5} \) J in the energy when the slab is removed (and an increase by the same amount when it is introduced).
note: The question asks for the change when the slab is REMOVED; the solution gave the change on inserting it. Now -48e-5 J (a decrease).

solution:
As shown in the figures at the end of this answer, suppose the two point charges are placed on \( x \)-axis with the positive charge located at the origin O.

\( q_1 = 5 \times 10^{-8} \) C at O, \( q_2 = -3 \times 10^{-8} \) C at A, with P between them; \( \text{OP} = x \), \( \text{PA} = 0.16 - x \), \( \text{OA} = 0.16 \) m.

Let the potential be zero at the point P and \( \text{OP} = x \). For \( x < 0 \) (i.e. to the left of O), the potentials of the two charges cannot add up to zero. Clearly, \( x \) must be positive. If \( x \) lies between O and A, then \( V_1 + V_2 = 0 \), where \( V_1 \) and \( V_2 \) are the potentials at point P due to O and A, respectively. The other possibility is that \( x \) may also lie on extended OA.

\( q_1 = 5 \times 10^{-8} \) C at O, \( q_2 = -3 \times 10^{-8} \) C at A, with P beyond A; \( \text{OA} = 0.16 \) m, \( \text{AP} = (x - 0.16) \) m.

\( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{q_1}{x} + \dfrac{q_2}{0.16 - x}\right] = 0 \)

\( 9 \times 10^{9}\left[\dfrac{5 \times 10^{-8}}{x} - \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-8}}{0.16 - x}\right] = 0 \)

\( \Rightarrow 9 \times 10^{9} \times 10^{-8}\left[\dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{3}{0.16 - x}\right] = 0 \)

\( \Rightarrow \dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{3}{0.16 - x} = 0 \)

\( \therefore x = 0.10 \) m, between the charges.

For P beyond A, \( \text{AP} = x - 0.16 \), so

\( \dfrac{5}{x} - \dfrac{3}{x - 0.16} = 0 \Rightarrow 5x - 0.8 = 3x \)

\( \therefore x = 0.40 \) m

The potential is zero at two points on the line: 10 cm and 40 cm from the positive charge.
note: The question asks for point(s) and the solution set up the case beyond A but never solved it: x = 0.40 m added.

solution:
**Data:** \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -36x\) (SI units). **To find:** \(n\) and \(T\).

The differential equation of linear S.H.M. is

\(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\omega^2 x\)

Comparing this with the given equation \(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -36x\),

\(\omega^2 = 36\ \text{s}^{-2} \Rightarrow \omega = 6\ \text{rad/s}\)

**Frequency:**

\(n = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{6}{2\pi} = \dfrac{3}{\pi} = \dfrac{3}{3.142} = 0.9548\ \text{Hz}\)

**Period:**

\(T = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{3.142}{3} = 1.047\ \text{s}\)

**The frequency of the S.H.M. is \(n = \dfrac{3}{\pi} \approx 0.955\ \text{Hz}\) and its period is \(T = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.05\ \text{s}\).**

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key says the length DECREASES by 5.07 mm. The magnitude is right and the direction is inverted. A second's pendulum keeps \(T = 2\ \text{s}\) at both places, so \(L = gT^2/4\pi^2 = g/\pi^2\) and \(L\) is directly proportional to \(g\); raising \(g\) from 9.75 to \(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2\) takes \(L\) from 0.98788 m to 0.99295 m, an INCREASE of 5.07 mm. The sign follows from the chapter's own equation for the period of a simple pendulum and depends on no assumed constant.]

**Data:** second's pendulum, so \(T = 2\ \text{s}\); \(g_1 = 9.75\ \text{m/s}^2\), \(g_2 = 9.80\ \text{m/s}^2\). **To find:** change in length \(\Delta L\).

A second's pendulum takes one second for each swing between the extremes, so its period is \(T = 2\ \text{s}\) at **both** places.

From \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\),

\(L = \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{g \times 4}{4\pi^2} = \dfrac{g}{\pi^2}\)

With \(\pi^2 = 9.870\):

\(L_1 = \dfrac{9.75}{9.870} = 0.9878\ \text{m} = 98.78\ \text{cm}\)

\(L_2 = \dfrac{9.80}{9.870} = 0.9929\ \text{m} = 99.29\ \text{cm}\)

Change in length:

\(\Delta L = L_2 - L_1 = \dfrac{g_2 - g_1}{\pi^2} = \dfrac{9.80 - 9.75}{9.870} = \dfrac{0.05}{9.870}\)

\(\Delta L = 5.066 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 0.5066\ \text{cm}\)

**The length must be increased by \(5.07 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\), that is by about \(0.507\ \text{cm}\) (roughly \(5.1\ \text{mm}\)).** Since \(L \propto g\) for a fixed period, the larger value of \(g\) needs the **longer** pendulum, so this is an **increase** in length.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(6.324\ \text{cm/s}\). The magnitude is right and the UNIT is wrong by a factor of \(10^2\): at the centre of the path the whole energy is kinetic, so \(v = \sqrt{2E/m} = \sqrt{2 \times 40 / 2} = 6.324\ \text{m/s}\) (632.4 cm/s). A speed of 6.324 cm/s would imply a total energy of \(0.004\ \text{J}\), against the 40 J the question states.]

**Data:** \(m = 2\ \text{kg}\), total energy \(E = 40\ \text{J}\). **To find:** speed at the centre of the path.

The centre of the path is the **mean position**. There the potential energy is zero, so the whole of the total energy is kinetic, and the speed there is the maximum speed \(v_{\max}\).

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}m v_{\max}^2\)

\(40 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times v_{\max}^2\)

\(v_{\max}^2 = 40\ \text{m}^2\text{/s}^2\)

\(v_{\max} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} = 6.325\ \text{m/s}\)

**The speed of the body while crossing the centre of the path is \(2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.32\ \text{m/s}\).**
note: 2 x 3.162 = 6.324, while sqrt(40) = 6.3246; the 3.162 step dropped.

solution:
**Data:** \(B = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{Wb/m}^2\), \(I = 3 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{kg m}^2\), magnetic moment \(\mu = 3\ \text{A m}^2\).

A magnet vibrating in the plane of a uniform magnetic field performs angular S.H.M. with period

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{\mu B}}\)

**Step 1: the magnetic restoring couple per unit angular displacement.**

\(\mu B = 3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-5} = 4.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N m/rad}\)

**Step 2: period.**

\(\dfrac{I}{\mu B} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{4.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 6.25 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{s}^2\)

\(\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{\mu B}} = \sqrt{6.25 \times 10^{-2}} = 0.25\ \text{s}\)

\(T = 2\pi \times 0.25 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1.571\ \text{s}\)

**Step 3: frequency and number of oscillations per minute.**

\(n = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{1.571} = 0.6366\ \text{Hz}\)

Number of oscillations in one minute \(= 60n = \dfrac{60}{T} = \dfrac{60}{\pi/2} = \dfrac{120}{\pi}\)

\(= \dfrac{120}{\pi} = 38.20\)

\(\therefore\) the magnet performs about \(38\) oscillations per minute (period \(1.571\ \text{s}\), frequency \(0.6366\ \text{Hz}\)).
